scenes.name: The doorstep
scenes.title: A book carried into the campaign.
scenes.evidence: The later movement history describes personal canvassing and campaign workers carrying packages of cookbooks into the field. It places the publication alongside conversations with neighbours and everyday contacts.
scenes.interpretation: The cookbook could serve as a portable introduction to a political conversation.
scenes.limit: A retrospective account of campaign methods. It does not identify every visitor or purchaser, or prove that each conversation included a sale or changed a vote.
scenes.next: Verification scope: dated canvassers’ letters, route records and cookbook orders.
scenes.locator: History of Woman Suffrage, vol.VI (1922), Washington chapter XLVI, p.677; chapter-source note196.
scenes.inspection: Specified passage reviewed in Gutenberg transcription; original page image not checked.
scenes.question: Who could enter a political conversation through an ordinary visit?

scenes.name: The club meeting
scenes.title: A menu became a subject for discussion.
scenes.evidence: The same chapter reports suffrage-club programmes about food quality and the exhibition and discussion of model menus.
scenes.interpretation: Knowledge associated with household provision became material for collective discussion.
scenes.limit: The passage does not name particular meetings, count attendees or reproduce the menus. It does not establish that these programmes used a particular cookbook recipe.
scenes.next: Verification scope: club minutes, notices, programmes and displayed menus for a named meeting.
scenes.locator: History of Woman Suffrage, vol.VI (1922), chapter XLVI, p.677.
scenes.inspection: Specified passage reviewed in Gutenberg transcription; not a club-minute or original-image check.
scenes.question: How did practical household knowledge acquire a public audience?

scenes.name: The fair booth
scenes.title: Publishing, selling and recruiting met.
scenes.evidence: The history describes suffrage booths selling cookbooks, pins and pennants while collecting enrolment signatures. Its discussion then turns to publicity at Seattle’s 1909 Alaska-Yukon-Pacific Exposition.
scenes.interpretation: A booth brought material goods and opportunities for political participation into one setting.
scenes.limit: The account does not give transactions, recruitment totals or conversion rates. Do not assign every reported booth practice to the Exposition or treat signatures as votes.
scenes.next: Verification scope: a booth programme, sales account and enrolment record for the same dated event.
scenes.locator: History of Woman Suffrage, vol.VI (1922), chapter XLVI, pp.677–678.
scenes.inspection: Specified passage reviewed in Gutenberg transcription; no booth account or original-image check.
scenes.question: When did buying an object become an invitation to join?

scenes.name: The shared table
scenes.title: Hospitality left an account.
scenes.evidence: Eaton’s convention-expense statement records a daylight dinner costing $200, ticket receipts of $168 and a stated net cost of $32.
scenes.interpretation: Shared hospitality required resources as well as organisation. This dinner was a net expense in the reported account, not a demonstrated fundraiser.
scenes.limit: The statement does not supply the menu, number of diners, ticket price, seating or a record of conversations. It is separate from cookbook sales and the later banquet to DeVoe.
scenes.next: Verification scope: the convention programme, dinner tickets, catering invoice and attendee records.
scenes.locator: Eaton, Treasurer’s Report through 10 January 1911, attached Report of National Convention Expense, 1909, manuscript p.3; item14747, SL_devoe_000954.jpg; WSL Manuscripts, MS171, Box2.
scenes.inspection: Entire original page image visually checked; factual dinner lines and arithmetic checked.
scenes.question: What did it cost to bring people to the same table?

visualPolicy: Original modern schematic line drawings for navigation; not archival images or reconstructions. The scenes are thematic connections, not a proven chronological route or measured flow of money or influence.
